desc:
An ancestor of a node is any node on the path from the root down to its parent. Given a binary tree and a value target that occurs in it, return the values of all ancestors of the node holding target, ordered from the closest one (its parent) up to the root.

The root has no ancestors, so for the root the answer is the empty array [].

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right). A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For the tree below ([3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 0, 8, -1, -1, 7, 4]) and target = 7 the answer is [2, 5, 3].

        3
      /   \
     5     1
    / \   / \
   6   2 0   8
      / \
     7   4
constraints: All node values are distinct, so a value identifies exactly one node
The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: The ancestors of a node are exactly the nodes you pass on the way from the root to it. How can you remember that way?
Store, for every node, who its parent is. Then starting from the target you can follow parents until you reach the root.

Level order puts every parent before its children. For the k-th real node, its children are at array slots 2k+1 and 2k+2, so a single pass fills a parent array. Walk up from the target and collect the values.
editorial: Record the parent of every node once, then climb. The climb from the target to the root visits at most depth(target) nodes, which is exactly the answer. The parent array can be filled in one linear pass over the level-order array because each real node accounts for exactly two child slots.

A recursive search that returns true when the target is found in its subtree and appends the current node on the way back out produces the same list. It is just as fast but uses recursion depth up to n on skewed trees.
